doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Honesty with students about a career in music
summary: Piltzecker says he must be honest about the music business, jokes about it, and says he teaches creativity rather than making a living.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Yeah. What’s your take on the scenario where a parent comes to you and you’ve been teaching their son or daughter and the son or daughter wants to go into music full time. They want to be — they want to make it in the music business. And you may have an opinion about that depending on how you feel their talent level is. Are you able to be honest with them?

If I can’t be honest I’m not worth anything to them as a professor. My obligation is to be honest. My obligation is also to tell them what I know and to help arm them with as many skills as they can have to pursue their dreams and careers. Will I talk honestly about the nature of the business? Of course. It’s a horrendous way to make a living if you — in a lot of ways. It’s also a beautiful way to make a living. But yeah, any profession has to

deal with this. And you could make it drive you crazy. In a way I’m preparing these people for a profession — a profession that doesn’t exist. I mean all the jazz musicians go through that. What are you going to — you’re going to go pay for your kids’ college and health insurance for the next twenty years by playing a local club? Good luck. When there are like eight thousand people that play just as well as you and might be cuter and know the owner? I mean those are the realities of things. I talk about them and I say this is the way it is, but at the same time I talk about what I am privileged to do and I share it as best I can and maybe some of that enthusiasm comes — I mean some people are just born performers. I get students, they’re going to do this. No matter how crazy it is, they’re going to do this. But I will help them and you know that’s my job as well as to be an artist. So I think the honesty is important. I can follow up with a joke, this is a stupid joke but I’ll tell you. So a young guy comes up and asks his dad, “Dad, when I grow up I want to be a jazz musician.” The father says, “Well son, you can’t do both.”

I don’t know if that’s relevant or not but I wish I had a great answer to fix this dilemma. I mean obviously it’s a societal problem and I could level my opinions about what the difference is between here and in Europe and about where we’re going culturally in this country and world-wide. That’s just not, it’s not going to fix the problem.

I’ve had a little — some dilemmas over the years with certain players who are really quite accomplished and they want to pursue this. And I’m torn about focusing on making them — continuing on the path of being the best player on their instrument they can, as opposed to the approach well if you want to make a living in music you have to be a good player but you also ought to, like okay, you should learn the piano. You should learn to take horn parts off the record. You should learn to do X and Y and Z and you’ll have a better chance of actually making a living than if you’re just a great saxophone player.

I agree. And I think I’ve been lucky and perhaps a little selfish to extract myself from that responsibility of taking it upon myself how to teach them how to make a living. Because it’s not the best thing I could do for them. I think the best thing I could do for them, my students, is to share my love of what I do and tell them all I know about the best — as honestly as I can. I think there are other people that can do that much better than I, and I agree with you, coming out equipped to make a living is a different skill. But I think, at least what I try to do is to help people, like my wife does, find more about their creative self, and find that fulfillment and the joy of being able to you know, create something artistically and share it and get the satisfaction from it. That’s something I can try to help people do better than making a living. And I’m not — in a certain sense I’m skirting the
responsibility but that’s not what I do best. You know? That’s not what I do best I don’t think.
